newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Opinion polls show NZ election too close to call.
newsitem.headline: Opinion polls show NZ election too close to call.

text.p: New Zealand's conservative National Party government surged five points in an opinion poll published on Sunday but may fall tantalisingly short of the support it needs to win re-election next month.
A TV1 poll showed National up five points at 40 percent while the main opposition Labour Party remained far back in second place on 18 percent, up two.

New Zealand will hold its first election under proportional representation on October 12, and National and its potential coalition partners are looking to win at least half the vote to form a stable majority government.

One possible partner, the radical free-market ACT New Zealand, scored five percent in the TV1 poll. Another, the morals-based Christian Coalition, had 4.5 percent -- short of the five percent needed to be sure of making it into parliament.
TV1 said National, ACT and the centrist United Party, which looks set to win one local constituency seat, could muster 59 of the 120 seats if the poll's results held through election night.
Labour, economic nationalist New Zealand First and the left-wing Alliance would have 61.
National, in power since 1990, has presided over a strong economic recovery and cut taxes in July, while still running budget surpluses and paying off national debt.

Its opponents say government policies are widening the gap between rich and poor. Labour and the Alliance, especially, promise higher funding of health and education, which many voters regard as the dominant election issues.
A poll on Saturday in the New Zealand Herald newspaper was gloomier for the government, which fell 2.8 percent to 36.8 while Labour rose five to 21.8 percent.
The Herald poll would give Labour, New Zealand First and the Alliance 69 seats out of 120.

Labour has displayed fresh confidence in recent days since a televised debate in which leader Helen Clark performed strongly. Clark could become New Zealand's first woman prime minister if the opposition parties can bridge policy differences and set aside personal feuds to form a stable government.
